stories.headline: STRAIT OF HORMUZ EFFECTIVELY CLOSED AS U.S., IRAN TRADE TANKER STRIKES OVER LABOR DAY WEEKEND
stories.body: The Strait of Hormuz is effectively closed to commercial shipping after the U.S. and Iran traded a fresh round of attacks over the weekend: CENTCOM permanently disabled two Iranian tankers and destroyed a third under a new 'tanker-for-tanker' policy approved by President Trump, hours after Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps fired ballistic missiles at a U.S. carrier and destroyer that both evaded harm. U.S. cash equity and bond markets are closed for Labor Day, so none of this is priced into stocks yet — Tuesday's reopen is the first chance for the S&P 500 to react.
stories.explain: Formal U.S. exchange closures don't stop global oil trading: Brent and WTI both trade nearly continuously on ICE and CME's Globex system, so crude was already marking the escalation higher through the holiday even with NYSE and NYMEX pit sessions dark. That gap between an always-on commodity market and a market-hours-only equity market is exactly why Tuesday's open often looks like it's 'catching up' to a weekend's news in one move rather than drifting into it gradually.

stories.headline: WTI TOPS $92, BRENT NEARS $98 AS HORMUZ RISK PREMIUM WIDENS INTO THE HOLIDAY
stories.body: WTI crude climbed above $92 a barrel and Brent approached $98 in global trading over the weekend as the tanker war intensified, extending a roughly $7 weekly gain driven by falling Iranian exports and the widening Hormuz risk premium. Both benchmarks had dipped to session lows near $89.30 (WTI) and $94.65 (Brent) earlier in the week before snapping back hard on the latest strikes.
stories.explain: Oil's move here is a pure geopolitical risk premium, not a supply or demand shift — no barrels have actually left the market yet, but traders are pricing in the probability that a fifth of global seaborne crude could be disrupted. That premium feeds directly into Thursday's CPI print: a sustained move above $90 WTI shows up in the energy component within one to two months, which is why a supply shock like this complicates the Fed's already-split rate debate.

stories.headline: MARKETS ENTER TUESDAY'S REOPEN STILL DIGESTING FRIDAY'S BLOWOUT JOBS REPORT
stories.body: With Monday's Labor Day holiday closing U.S. equity and bond markets, the S&P 500 (7,718.60, -0.38%) and Treasury market carry Friday's reaction to August's blowout payrolls print — 162,000 jobs added versus 53,000 expected, unemployment steady at 4.1% — into Tuesday's session. The report flipped the market's read from 'the Fed can ease' to 'the Fed may need to hold or hike,' the exact dynamic investors will keep testing when trading resumes.
stories.explain: A holiday close freezes the tape but not the flow of information: any data or news that lands after Friday's close — like the weekend's Hormuz escalation — gets absorbed into Tuesday's single reopening print instead of being smoothed across a normal trading day. That's why the first hour of a post-holiday session often carries outsized volume and volatility relative to an ordinary Tuesday.

stories.headline: FED RATE-HIKE ODDS HOLD NEAR A COIN FLIP HEADING INTO THIS MONTH'S FOMC MEETING
stories.body: CME FedWatch pricing for a 25 bp hike at this month's FOMC meeting remains roughly split after spiking to 58.4% on Friday's jobs report before Fed Governor Christopher Waller's remarks favoring a hold if disinflation resumes pulled odds back toward 50%. The 2-year Treasury yield, at 4.37% after Friday's close, sits at its highest level since January 2025 and will be the first real read on where that debate stands once trading resumes Tuesday.
stories.explain: Fed funds futures convert directly into implied hike/cut probabilities because each contract settles against the average effective fed funds rate for its delivery month, so a shift in the contract price is a shift in the market's expected policy path. A near-50/50 split this close to a meeting is unusual — it signals the committee itself, not just the market, is genuinely undecided, which raises the stakes on every data point and speaker between now and the decision.

stories.headline: LULULEMON'S 17% SLIDE STILL WEIGHS ON RETAIL AS SHARES ENTER THE WEEK NEAR MULTI-YEAR LOWS
stories.body: Lululemon closed Friday down 17.4% at $100.61 after Q2 revenue of $2.42 billion missed estimates, comparable sales fell 9-10% with North America comps down 12%, and management cut full-year revenue guidance to a 5-7% decline — leaving the stock off roughly 42% year-to-date heading into Tuesday's session.
stories.explain: Guidance cuts move stocks more than the trailing quarter because equity value is a claim on future cash flows, not past ones — a 5-7% revenue decline reset for next year re-prices every future quarter's earnings base, not just the one just reported. Lululemon's five-month gap between naming a new CEO in April and their September 8 start date compounded the problem by leaving the company without clear leadership through the exact stretch its core business was deteriorating.

stories.headline: DEFENDING CHAMP MICHIGAN SLIDES IN EARLY POLLS AFTER LOSING FIVE-STAR BIG MAN TO INJURY
stories.body: March's national champion Michigan dropped in CBS Sports' early Top 25 And 1 rankings after five-star freshman big man Brandon McCoy Jr. went down with an injury, while preseason polls continue shifting across outlets as the transfer portal window closes. Four-star 2027 guard Tre Keith's commitment to Boston College over Mississippi State and Clemson was among the weekend's headline recruiting moves.

stories.headline: KAWHI LEONARD-TO-RAPTORS TRADE DETAILS REVEALED: CLIPPERS GET BRANDON INGRAM, GRADEY DICK, FIVE PICKS
stories.body: With the trade appearing imminent pending final league paperwork, reported terms have Toronto sending Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, and a package of picks — unprotected 2031 and 2033 firsts, 2030 and 2033 seconds, and a 2027 first-round swap — to the Clippers for Kawhi Leonard, who returns to the franchise he led to the 2019 title now that L.A.'s salary-cap circumvention penalties have cleared the way.

stories.headline: TUA TAGOVAILOA OFFICIALLY NAMED FALCONS' WEEK 1 STARTER OVER INJURED MICHAEL PENIX JR.
stories.body: Atlanta officially handed the keys to its offense to Tua Tagovailoa for the season opener against Pittsburgh, signed on a one-year, near-minimum deal after Miami released him, while first-round pick Michael Penix Jr. continues recovering from a season-ending ACL injury. It sets up a quarterback competition to watch once Penix is healthy, with Atlanta running a bridge plan at the position for 2026.

stories.headline: MICHIGAN NEEDS CONTROVERSIAL HAIL MARY TO ESCAPE WESTERN MICHIGAN 13-12 AS LSU ROUTS CLEMSON 51-10
stories.body: Michigan avoided a Week 1 upset only after an extra second was put back on the clock for a game-winning Hail Mary against Western Michigan, while LSU throttled Clemson 51-10 — holding the Tigers to -10 rushing yards at one point — and No. 1 Ohio State routed Ball State 56-3 behind Julian Sayin's 320 yards and three touchdowns. FCS upsets continued too, with Idaho State topping Utah State 29-17 for the season's third FCS-over-FBS win.

sports.detail: No. 17 Washington beat Washington State 24-10 in the 118th Apple Cup Sunday at Husky Stadium; Demond Williams Jr. threw for 268 yards and a touchdown and added a 5-yard rushing score. Washington leads the all-time series 78-34-6 and hosts Utah State next Saturday, Sept. 12.

Texas Tech transfer LeJuan Watts (11.8 pts, 6.0 reb last season) and guard Harun Zrno, formerly of Rutgers, continue building out Danny Sprinkle's third roster; Wesley Yates III returns as the team's leading returning scorer. On the women's side, Sayvia Sellers dropped 24 points in an 84-75 win over Illinois to sweep UW's first Big Ten road trip.

The defending Super Bowl LX champs host New England in Wednesday's NFL Kickoff Game (5:20 PM PT, NBC) at Lumen Field — a rematch of Seattle's 29-13 title-game win. Seattle's 53-man roster is set, with newly signed OT Bobby Hart on an early practice squad.

Jalen Duren's restricted free agency standoff drags into September — Detroit's five-year offer (~$35M/year) remains roughly $5M annually below the third-team All-NBA center's ask of $40M+. Season opens at Boston, Tuesday, Oct. 20.

Seattle (67-78, 3rd in the AL West) beat Oakland 2-0 Sunday behind eight scoreless innings and nine strikeouts from Bryan Woo, salvaging the finale of a series they otherwise dropped. Off Monday, they host Texas Tuesday to open a new series.

watchlist: Markets reopen Tuesday after Labor Day — first chance for the S&P 500 to price in the weekend's Hormuz escalation and Friday's blowout jobs report
CPI data Thursday — watch for early pass-through from oil's move above $90 WTI into the energy component
FOMC meeting this month — rate-hike odds sitting near a coin flip after Waller's push-back on Friday's payrolls beat
Seahawks host New England in the NFL Kickoff Game — Wednesday, Sept. 9, Lumen Field, Super Bowl LX rematch
Mariners host Texas — Tuesday, Sept. 8, T-Mobile Park, looking to build on Sunday's shutout win

deepDive.title: Why Oil Keeps Trading When Wall Street Doesn't: Continuous Markets and the Holiday Gap
content: Today is Labor Day, so the NYSE, Nasdaq, and U.S. Treasury market are all closed — yet WTI and Brent both moved sharply higher over the weekend as the U.S. and Iran traded tanker strikes in the Strait of Hormuz. That asymmetry, where one market freezes while another keeps repricing in real time, is the most useful lens for understanding what Tuesday's reopen will actually look like. It won't be a fresh reaction to a single headline; it will be equities catching up all at once to everything that happened while they were shut.

The mechanism is straightforward: crude trades nearly continuously through ICE (Brent) and CME's Globex system (WTI), each with only a brief nightly technical reset, while listed U.S. equities only trade during set exchange hours and close entirely on holidays like Labor Day. Geopolitical risk doesn't pause for a calendar, so continuous futures markets let new information get priced the moment it happens — which is exactly how WTI reached above $92 and Brent neared $98 this weekend without a single U.S. stock trading. Equity index futures, like the E-mini S&P, trade nearly as continuously and function as the bridge that lets traders gauge Monday's news before Tuesday's cash open.

What's easy to miss is that a post-holiday gap isn't noise — it's information that had nowhere else to go. In October 1987, a weekend of overseas selling and a dollar policy dispute compounded into Black Monday partly because U.S. markets had no continuous mechanism to absorb the news gradually; more recent holiday gaps, like moves following weekend Middle East strikes in past years, show the same pattern at smaller scale: futures markets do the price discovery first, and the cash market's opening print is really just it catching up. The size of that gap is a direct measure of how much information built up during the closure.

For Tuesday, that means the S&P's opening move should be read as one combined reaction to both Friday's jobs report and the weekend's Hormuz escalation, not a clean signal about either one in isolation — expect elevated volume and volatility in the first hour as the market sorts out which story is driving price. It also raises the stakes on Thursday's CPI print: oil's move is already embedded in futures markets days before it can show up in a government inflation release, so by the time CPI prints, the market will already have partially traded the outcome it's supposed to measure.
